question: On 3 April 2025, the Hungarian Government announced its withdrawal from the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (ICC). In May 2025, Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, Kaja Kallas, indicated that the Commission was analysing Hungary’s announced withdrawal in the light of the EU acquis1.

Hungary is currently bound by the Rome Statute, and has been referred to the Assembly of States Parties for non-compliance with the ICC arrest warrant against Benjamin Netanyahu during his visit from 2 to 6 April 20252. 1.

With regard to the analysis, can the Commission clarify: (a) whether the analysis is still ongoing and, if so, whether the results will be shared with Parliament and the public; (b) whether the analysis has been terminated or paused and, if so, why; and (c) whether the Commission can commit to publishing the results, including its conclusion on the potential violation of the EU acquis, before Hungary’s withdrawal enters into force on 2 June 20263?
Does the Commission agree with Parliament’s assessment4 that withdrawal from the Rome Statute would violate the EU acquis, including Articles 2 and 4(3) of the Treaty on European Union?
Will the Commission publicly denounce Hungary’s failure to comply with the ICC arrest warrant against Benjamin Netanyahu, considering his second planned visit on 21 March 20265?

answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.7.2026) The EU remains a steadfast supporter of international criminal justice, particularly the International Criminal Court (ICC), in its mission to ensure accountability for the most serious crimes under international law.

The EU has consistently called upon all States to ensure full cooperation with the ICC to comply with their obligations under international law and as State Parties to the Rome Statute, including by the prompt execution of outstanding arrest warrants, and to protect the Court’s impartiality and independence in the pursuit of accountability around the world.

The EU will continue to cooperate with the ICC in the framework of their Agreement on cooperation and assistance1, including, pursuant to Article 6 of the Agreement, by adopting initiatives to promote the dissemination of the principles, values and provisions of the Statute.

Article 127 of the Rome Statute allows for states to withdraw from the ICC, by written notification addressed to the Secretary-General of the UN. However, withdrawal takes effect one year after notification of the depositary. The withdrawing State is obliged to continue fulfilling its obligations (financial obligations and obligations of cooperation with the ICC).

In this context, the EU notes that the government of Hungary recently announced its intention to reverse the decision to withdraw from the Rome Statute, and that Parliament voted on 27 May 2026 on a bill to revoke Hungary’s withdrawal from the ICC, which was notified by Hungary to the Secretary-General of the United Nations on 29 May 2026.
